DeWitt’s father’s mother, Barbara Hammond, came of three migrations.
The Hammonds, Hamants of Medfield in the 1600s, moved west a step at a time.
Hinsdale Hammond of Sturbridge, a soldier of the Revolution, moved to Wardsboro,
Vermont, where his son Selah was born in 1796, and about 1816 Selah came on to build a sawmill on Mead’s Creek at
Campbell, in Steuben County, New York. By 1860 Abel Hammond was across the state line in McKean County,
Pennsylvania, timber country that was soon to be oil country.
The Trettons were Irish, from the south-west by their names: John Tretton's mother was a Bresnahan,
and his wife Catherine was a Kelleher, sister of a lieutenant who died serving at Fort Davis,
Texas. They left Ireland after 1863, in the long emigration that followed the Famine,
spent a few years in Massachusetts, and came on to Turtle Point in McKean County,
where their daughter Katherine married Edward J. Hammond.
Around 1910 Edward took the family to New Kensington, on the Allegheny above Pittsburgh,
and worked in its tin mill for the rest of his working life.
The Seiferths were Bavarian: Henry Seiferth followed his brothers to Pittsburgh in 1886,
while its mills were drawing immigrants by the tens of thousands, and became a wholesale whiskey dealer there.
